>

*This version keeps closer to the original fragmented structure and poetic rhythm while refining the grammar, punctuation, and word choice for a sleek, atmospheric feel.*

>

**In honor of Max Rojas:**

Every month, when the lunar cycle strips the night sky completely bare, Don Max hauls a seat down to the ocean’s edge. Along this dark-sanded shore, a green-backed heron is present. Shedding her pearlescent ornaments, the personified moon laments that she has been reduced to mere stark monochrome and keeps misplacing her own visage. 

Reaching into his garments, Don Max feels around for his pipe, draws it out, and taps it against the palm of his hand. The moon wails about her advanced age, complaining that the nighttime chill gives her skin bumps. While Don Max searches for his smoking leaf, he manages to locate a fire stick. The moon remarks on how agonizingly hard it is to reconstruct oneself out of total emptiness. Don Max simply grins and ignites his smoke. 

She admits her tendency to repeat the same errors and advises him to abandon her. Peering through the rising haze, she watches Don Max shape a strand of kelp into an insect. She demands that he depart for his own well-being, while Don Max places the newly crafted seaweed grasshopper onto the beach sand. Melancholically, as if the fact brings her grief, she adds that her overwhelming charm is another obstacle, insisting she will eventually seek new companions and erase all recollection of him.

Once a month, when the moon begins her agonizing wane, Don Max carries a weathered wooden chair down to the edge of the sea. He settles at the tide line where the water laps against the obsidian grains of a black sand beach, waiting patiently in the darkness for a quiet, ethereal dialogue to begin. 

High above the restless ocean, the waning moon pours out her profound distress. Her voice, like a cool silver breeze across the water, drips with sorrow as she laments the cruel absurdity of her existence. She speaks of her relentless, repeating cycles—the agony of reaching full, radiant perfection only to feel her identity dissolve, her body age, and her warmth fade slice by slice until she is consumed by total darkness. She grieves the terror of becoming a ghost of herself, doomed to forget who she was each time she shrinks away.

Through her existential grief, Don Max maintains a calm, unshakeable presence. He offers no empty promises or grand speeches, knowing that some sorrows simply demand a witness. With practiced, quiet motions, he strikes a match—its fleeting orange glow illuminating his lined face—and lights his pipe. He listens deeply, exhaling sweet clouds of smoke that drift upward into the night air as an offering to her pain.

Seeing the old man bound to her suffering, the moon’s panic turns to worry for her companion. She insists that Don Max should leave her, urging him to return to the safety of his home for his own good. "It is not right for a mortal to sit with such decay," she whispers. Yet, Don Max remains steadfast. As she pleads with him to go, she watches his calloused hands reach into the wet sand, pull up a slick strip of dark kelp, and carefully fold it. With delicate precision, he bends the wet green ribbon until it takes the unmistakable shape of a small grasshopper resting in his palm.

Her heart breaks at his gentle devotion, but the moon’s sorrow only deepens into a painful truth. She mournfully warns him that her tragic, irresistible beauty is a curse. When she rises again, full and bright, her light will inevitably attract other lovers, poets, and dreamers to her shores. "I am bound to the sky, Max," she whispers, her crescent sliver growing fainter by the second. "I will shine for others, and when the dark takes me again, I will eventually forget you."

Don Max does not flinch. He simply holds the seaweed grasshopper close, sitting motionless on the black sand as the final sliver of light slips away, content to love her even in the shadow of being forgotten.
outputs.L4:
The night air off the coast was crisp and laden with salt, carrying the distant, low roar of the tide as it dragged over wet pebbles. High above the ink-black expanse of the Pacific, the moon was shrinking. 

She was entering her late waning phase, her once-round, pearlescent face eroded to a sharp, brittle crescent. To the world below, she was simply following her celestial schedule, but to herself, she was dying. Panic rippled across her fading light. She felt thin, hollowed out, and stripped of the blinding radiance that had commanded the ocean just a week before. The shadow crept across her cheek like a stain of dark ink, a terrifying reminder of her vanity, her mortality, and the inevitable void that awaited her at the end of every month.

"Look at me!" she wailed, her voice echoing in the chill wind that whipped the crests of the waves. "I am dissolving! My light is rotting away! Look away, dark ocean, look away, sky! Leave me to vanish in peace! I cannot bear to be seen like this!"

Down on the shore, sitting on a log of bleached driftwood, Don Max did not cover his eyes. 

He was an old man whose face bore its own topography of lines—wrinkles carved by decades of sun, wind, and silent contemplation. He wore a heavy wool sweater smelling of salt and old cedar. As the moon thrashed in her sky-bound agony, dramatic and weeping, Don Max struck a wooden match against a dry stone. 

The small, orange flame illuminated his weathered knuckles for a moment before he applied it to the bowl of his wooden pipe. He drew deeply, the tobacco crackling faintly, and exhaled a thick ring of sweet, pale smoke into the cool air. The smoke drifted upward, briefly veiling the moon’s sharp, panicked beam.

"Did you not hear me, old man?" the moon cried, her voice sharpening with defensive pride. "Turn your back! I am a shadow of myself! I am ugly, diminished, dying! Leave me alone!"

Don Max did not answer with grand speeches. He didn't even look up to lecture her on astronomy or the nature of orbit. Instead, he reached down into the damp sand near his boots and picked up a long, dark strip of sea-kelp that had washed ashore with the evening tide. 

Slowly, deliberately, he began to work with his hands. 

His movements were smooth, unhurried, and deeply grounded, forming an anchor against the frantic energy above. He folded the slippery, rubbery strand over itself. *Loop. Tuck. Crease.* The ocean hissed against the shore, a steady rhythm that matched the rising and falling of his chest. 

The moon paused her lamentations, drawn despite herself to the quiet rhythm on the sand. "What are you doing?" she whispered, her dramatic fury faltering into cold curiosity. "Why do you sit there while I unravel?"

Don Max puffed gently on his pipe, the red ember glowing softly in the dark like a tiny, earthbound star. He bent a section of the seaweed back to form a long, slender leg, then another. With nimble, calloused fingers, he shaped a body, a head, and two delicate, arching antennae. 

He was folding the discarded ocean vegetation into a grasshopper.

He placed the finished creature carefully on the flat top of the driftwood log beside him. It sat there, glistening dark green in the moon's dim, dying light—a fragile piece of trash transformed by patience into an instrument of art.

"You spend so much time fearing the shadow," Don Max finally spoke, his voice low and raspy, like stones tumbling in a gentle surf. He didn't look up, but his tone was brimming with an enduring tenderness. "You think because you are small tonight, you are gone. But the tide comes in, and the tide goes out. The grasshopper dies in the autumn, but the song stays in the grass."

He took another long drag from his pipe, resting his hands in his lap. 

"I have watched you grow fat with light, *mi luna*, and I have watched you shrink to a sliver a thousand times," he said softly. "You are not fading. You are just breathing out. And I will be sitting right here when you breathe back in."

The moon stared down at the small seaweed grasshopper resting on the driftwood, and then at the old man bathed in her faint, imperfect glow. Her dramatic rage melted into a soft, aching quiet. The terrifying void ahead of her didn't seem quite so vast when measured against the steady, unbothered presence of the man below. 

She did not hide behind a cloud. She did not scream for the dark to claim her. Instead, she hung there in the quiet night, small and pale, letting her dim light rest upon Don Max's shoulders as he smoked his pipe in the dark, waiting patiently for the cycle to turn once more.

The worn leather package sat on the mahogany desk, its edges frayed by time and travel. On the front, written in a bold, elegant script that had barely faded over the decades, were just three words: **For Max Rojas**.

Max stared at the package, the sound of the rain tapping against his study window filling the quiet room. At seventy-two, Max Rojas was a man accustomed to silence and routine. He had spent the better part of his life as a restorer of ancient maps, living quietly in a coastal town where the air always smelled of salt and old paper. He was a keeper of forgotten routes, yet he had never expected a piece of his own past to find its way back to him.

He picked up a brass letter opener and carefully cut the twine. 

Inside lay a heavy, tarnished silver pocket watch and a leather-bound journal. Max’s hands trembled slightly as he opened the watch. On the inner casing, an inscription was carved into the metal: *“Time is only a river. Meet me at the bend.”*

He recognized the handwriting immediately. It belonged to Mateo, a childhood friend with whom he had explored the dusty hills of Santiago fifty years ago, before life, politics, and distance had pulled them apart. 

Max opened the journal. The first page contained a single paragraph written specifically **for** him:

> *“If you are reading this, Max, it means the sea finally brought my promise home to you. We spent our youth searching for wild places, but the greatest journey was always the one we left unfinished. The compass points south. The rest is **for Max Rojas** to discover.”*

A smile tugged at the corner of Max’s mouth. For years, he had believed that his adventurous spirit had faded, replaced by the quiet comfort of his books and maps. But holding the weight of the silver watch, feeling the textured paper of Mateo’s journal, he felt a spark long thought extinguished.

He walked over to the window and looked out at the mist rising from the ocean. The world was still vast, still full of mysteries waiting to be untangled. 

Max closed his eyes, took a deep breath, and began to pack a bag. The map of his life was not yet complete.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem dedicated to Max Rojas about an old man named Don Max who sits on a black sand beach once a month to listen to the new moon speak while he smokes his pipe.
counterfactuals.output:
*For Max Rojas, who knew that the deepest waters are those that swallow the light, and that silence has its own heavy, rolling syntax.*

Once every moonless turn, when the sky folds its linen and hides the white plate of the moon, Don Max descends to the edge of the basalt coast. He moves slowly, a silhouette carved from old oak and stubborn salt, stepping onto a beach of pure obsidian sand—grains of volcanic night, cool and heavy, crushed beneath his boots like powdered star-shards. He sits upon a bleached root of driftwood, facing the invisible horizon where the black water meets the blacker air, and pulls a briar pipe from his coat.

He strikes a match. For a second, a small, violent sun flares between his calloused thumbs, illuminating his face—a map of deep canyons and patient waiting—before the wind snaps it out. But the tobacco catches. A small red eye winks in the dark. Don Max draws the smoke deep into his chest, holding the warm, earthy leaf against his lungs, then releases a slow plume of grey ribbon that dissolves into the wet Atlantic gale.

He does not look for the moon; he knows she is there, an unlit mouth hanging in the rafters of the night. He comes only to listen. 

When the moon is new, she does not shine; she speaks. Her voice is not a sound, but a pulling—a low, resonant hum that rattles in the hollow of his ribcage and echoes in the marrow of his shins. She speaks of the great abyssal South, of drowned cathedrals and unwritten elegies, of the endless, beautiful weight of things that exist without needing to be seen. She speaks in the dialect of tides and roots, telling him that darkness is not the absence of light, but its origin; that memory is just a fire we tend until the ash becomes smooth as velvet.

Don Max puffs steadily, the red coal of his pipe rising and falling like a tide of one. He listens to the invisible sphere whisper her secrets to the black shore, nodding twice into the gloom. He asks for nothing. He brings no grief that the salt cannot wash clean. He simply sits until the tobacco turns to silver ash, sharing the quiet communion of old, heavy things—the ocean, the earth, the dark, and a man who has learned the patient art of breathing in the void.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal piece of magical realism poetry featuring a conversation between a quiet man and a dramatic, personified moon that is losing her light. Include imagery like milkglass earrings, pipe smoke, and seaweed.
counterfactuals.output:
She stepped down from the canopy of midnight
and sat upon his porch rail, gasping,
her velvet gown reeking of the trench and the surge.
Black, slick strands of seaweed were coiled at her ankles,
dragged from the ocean bed when her gravity gave out.

"I am extinguishing, darling," she swooned,
a hand pressed dramatically against her collarbone.
"The sun has bled me dry! The stars are whispering! 
Look at what the sky has reduced me to!"

Her glow was sputtering—a theatrical lamp 
starved of oil, turning from quicksilver to bruised tin. 

The quiet man did not leap up. He only sat in his wicker chair,
struck a match against the sole of his boot,
and brought the flame to the bowl of his briar pipe.
A thick curl of sweet, cherry-scented pipe smoke rose between them,
hanging in the air like a grey silk curtain
to veil her tragic, fading face.

"You always did prefer a grand exit," he said softly,
his voice low and slow, like stones rolling under a gentle wave.

"It is not an exit, it is a tragedy!" she wept.
Her tears fell onto the floorboards as tiny, hard pearls that rolled away.
With trembling, luminous fingers, 
she unclasped her milkglass earrings—
two heavy, opaque globes that had lost their inner fire.
She pressed them into his calloused palm.
"Keep them," she whispered. "Remember me when I am only chalk."

The man looked at the milkglass, cool and smooth in his hand.
He blew another ring of smoke into the dark;
it drifted toward her head and hovered there,
a soft, dark crown to replace her dying halo.

"The sea still knows your name," he told her,
pointing to the kelp bound around her wrists, 
which was beginning to hum with pale bioluminescence.
"And the dark isn't a grave. It's just a room where you can rest."

The moon sighed—a sound like dry leaves swept across marble—
and leaned her heavy, dimming head against his wool-clad shoulder.
She gave up her last bright ray with a soft, dramatic flutter of her wrists,
letting the night drink her light until she was only a silhouette 
smelling of salt, oakum, and smoke.

And the quiet man stayed very still,
smoking his pipe in the absolute dark,
listening to the seaweed breathe upon the wood.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a melancholic prose poem about aging, beauty, and memory? I'd like it to take place on a dark beach at night with a man named Don Max and a green-backed heron, where the moon speaks about how hard it is to come back from nothing.
counterfactuals.output:
Don Max carries his bones across the wet, iron-colored tide-line, each heavy step a small confession to the sand. The ocean is a dark, restless mouth swallowing its own foam, and the night air smells of kelp, cold salt, and the slow, inevitable decay of the shore. Don Max remembers when his skin was a map of midday sun, when love was a sudden, easy storm that left him breathless, but now he is only the outline of a man—a hollow husk where memories rattle like dry pebbles in a tin. He wonders where beauty goes when the body sheds it. Does it dissolve into the sea spray, or does it sink into the black depth, forever out of reach?

A few paces away, hunched like a folded secret at the water’s edge, stands a green-backed heron. In the light of day, its feathers are the polished moss of ancient riverbanks, a sudden, breath-taking iris of emerald and bronze hidden beneath a quiet cap. Tonight, in the velvet dark, it is a stillness deeper than the tide, a silhouette of infinite patience waiting for a flash of silver beneath the black waves. Don Max envies the bird. The heron does not grieve the sunlight; it simply wears the dark like a second plumage, holding the memory of its own brilliance secretly against its ribs. 

Above them, the sky tears open, and the moon pulls herself slowly from the navy throat of the clouds. She is thin and scarred, a sliver of bone-light spilling a cold, milky dust across the heron’s back and the old man’s weathered face. Her voice does not fall from above, but rises from the foam at their feet, low and heavy as a shifting reef. 

*“You grieve the loosening of your flesh, Don Max,”* the moon sighs, her pale light trembling on the black water. *“You mourn the eyes that no longer catch the light, the hands that have forgotten how to hold a shape. But you know nothing of the true shadow. You do not know how exhausting it is to vanish completely, to be erased by the sky, and then to drag oneself out of the dark again. You do not know how hard it is to come back from nothing, to carve light out of absolute silence, night after night, just to prove you were once whole.”*

Don Max closes his eyes. The wind pulls at his thin hair, carrying the sharp, cold scent of the deep sea. Beside him, the heron shifts its weight, a soft rustle of dark feathers, and together they listen to the roaring emptiness. The water laps at the man’s boots and the bird’s yellow feet, equalizing them in the cold, wet dark. Bathing in the moon’s painful, hard-won radiance, Don Max opens his hands to the night—learning, at last, that to have once been beautiful is a burden, but to remain standing in the dark, waiting for the light to return, is the only grace left.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

*For Max Rojas*

The tide retreats on the black sand beach,
leaving cold foam in its place,
beneath the draft of a restless wind
and a moon that keeps losing her face.

A thumb strikes flint; a pipe is lit,
a small red heart against the night,
as sweet smoke curls into the mist

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a quiet, poetic vignette about the monthly ritual of an old man sitting at the edge of the sea as the moon tries to break up with him.
counterfactuals.output:
Every twenty-nine days, she came back to tell him it was over. 

She was always at her most dramatic when she was full. Round, brilliant, and bloated with silver light, she hung low over the black shelf of the Atlantic, casting a gleaming, highway-wide tear across the water straight to where Arthur sat. 

Arthur pulled his wool coat tighter against the sea-chill. His boots were dusted with dry salt; his knees ached with the humidity. He unscrewed the cup of his thermos, the steam from his tea rising to join the low, wandering fog.

“I know,” he murmured into the wind. 

She began, as she always did, by shifting the tide. She pulled the water back, scraping heavy gravel across the shore with a long, harsh hiss—a woman gathering her skirts before turning to leave. 

*Look at us,* her light seemed to say, cold and sharp enough to cast his shadow clear against the wet shingle. *You are made of damp earth and slow blood. I am made of dust and impact craters. I belong to the orbit. I belong to the vacuum.*

Arthur took a sip of tea. It tasted of cardamom and metal. He looked at her—really looked at her—noticing the pale, bruised shadow of the Sea of Tranquility on her cheek. 

“You’ve said that before,” he said softly. 

She flared behind a thin ribbon of cirrus cloud, pretending to hide her face. *It isn’t you,* she insisted, translating her light into the rhythm of the waves crashing hard against the breaker stones. *It’s the physics. I am pulled by things you cannot see. I am shrinking, Arthur. I grow smaller every night from here on out. By next week, I will be a sliver. By the week after, I won’t even exist for you.*

“You’re just fading,” Arthur said. “You do it every month. You get tired.”

*I am leaving,* she insisted, her light growing colder, turning the foam on the beach into spilling mercury. *This time, I mean it. I am going into the dark, and I am not coming back.*

Arthur sighed, his breath a small, brief cloud that vanished instantly. He knew better than to argue with a full moon. She was ancient, but she was terribly young about endings. She believed every twilight was the final one; she believed every waning was a death.

He reached down and picked up a smooth, flat stone, cool as a coinslot, and tossed it into the surf. It disappeared into the dark ribs of the water. 

“I’ll be here,” he told the salt air. 

*Don’t wait for me,* she rasped, pulling a thick grey fog over her brow like a veil. Her brightness dulled to a bruised amber. *I am going to turn my face away. I am going to become nothing.*

Arthur didn't move. He watched as the fog slowly swallowed her rim, biting her down to an ember, then to a ghost, then to a pale, milky smudge behind the night. The sea grew dark and heavy, the silver road on the water dissolving until there was only the black, endless repetition of the swell.

He finished his tea. He shook the last drops out onto the stones, screwed the cup back onto the thermos, and stood up. His hips popped in the quiet. 

He turned his back on the sea and began the slow, uphill walk toward his small cottage, where the porch light burned yellow and warm. 

He didn't look back, because he didn't need to. He knew her drama. He knew her grief. And he knew that in twenty-nine days, thin and frail and full of quiet apologies, she would creep back to his window, waiting for him to walk down to the shore so she could tell him, all over again, how impossible it was for her to stay.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
